nameStory: The Broad-billed Hummingbird gets its name from its distinctively wide, bright red bill that's noticeably broader than most other hummingbird species. This wide bill helps it access nectar from flowers with different shapes and sizes. The scientific name 'latirostris' literally means 'broad-beaked' in Latin, reinforcing this key identifying feature.
description: The Broad-billed Hummingbird is a small, brilliantly colored hummingbird that's a rare visitor to New England, normally living in Mexico and the southwestern United States. Males are particularly striking with iridescent blue-green plumage, while females are more subdued with grayish coloring. Both sexes share the species' signature feature: a broad, bright red bill with a black tip. Like all hummingbirds, they're tiny birds, roughly 3-4 inches long with rapidly beating wings that create their characteristic humming sound.

idTips.label: Bill Shape and Color
idTips.description: Look for the distinctively broad, bright red bill with a black tip - noticeably wider than other hummingbirds and almost coral-colored in good light

idTips.label: Male Coloring
idTips.description: Males flash brilliant blue-green iridescent plumage on their throat and head that shimmers like metal in sunlight

idTips.label: Female Appearance
idTips.description: Females show grayish-brown upperparts with lighter underparts and the same characteristic broad red bill

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Hovers at flowers with wings beating so fast they're just a blur, creating a high-pitched humming or buzzing sound

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Most active during daylight hours, often seen darting aggressively between flowers or feeders

habitat: In New England, this would be an extremely rare vagrant far from its normal range. If spotted, it would most likely be at hummingbird feeders in residential areas, gardens with trumpet-shaped flowers, or woodland edges with flowering plants. Look near sugar water feeders, bee balm patches, or other nectar sources where it might stop during migration.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to appear, but any sighting would probably occur during spring migration when birds occasionally overshoot their normal range.
seasonality.summer: The most likely season for a rare vagrant to appear at feeders or flowering gardens, though still extraordinarily uncommon in New England.
seasonality.fall: Possible but very rare during fall migration when birds might wander eastward from their normal southwestern routes.
seasonality.winter: Would not survive New England winters; any winter sighting would be extremely unusual and noteworthy.

funFact: With only one recorded observation in all of New England, seeing a Broad-billed Hummingbird here would be like winning the birdwatching lottery - you'd be witnessing a bird that's roughly 2,000 miles outside its normal range!
confusionNotes: Could potentially be confused with Ruby-throated Hummingbirds, but the Broad-billed's distinctively wide, bright red bill (versus the Ruby-throat's thin, dark bill) makes identification straightforward. Remember: 'Broad bill, bright red' versus 'thin bill, dark thread.'
contextualKnowledge: This species highlights how bird ranges can occasionally produce surprising vagrants - individual birds that end up far from where they 'should' be. Any Broad-billed Hummingbird sighting in New England would be significant enough to report to eBird and local birding communities, as it represents an exceptional range extension.
compareHints: Since this is the only species in its genus found in North America, compare it to other hummingbirds in the region. Unlike the common Ruby-throated Hummingbird with its needle-thin dark bill, the Broad-billed has that unmistakable wide, coral-red bill. The male's blue-green iridescence is also more extensive than the Ruby-throat's focused red throat patch.
